Reading · the rules nobody explains

1.1 Discuss. What would a visitor to your country do wrong in the first week without realising it?

KEY WORDS

trivial small and unimportant

a newcomer a person who has just arrived

to interpret to work out what something means

modest small, not impressive

The Rules Nobody Tells You

Every culture has a set of rules that nobody writes down and everybody knows. You must not ask a British colleague how much they earn. In some countries you are supposed to refuse food twice before accepting it. In Japan you should never leave your chopsticks standing upright in a bowl of rice. None of this appears in a guidebook, because to the people who follow these rules they are not rules at all — they are simply how things are done.

This is why culture shock so rarely announces itself. Newcomers expect to struggle with the language and the food, and they usually manage both within a few months. What defeats them is smaller: a colleague who seems cold, a neighbour who never invites them in, a silence in a meeting that they cannot interpret. Each incident on its own is trivial. Twenty of them in a month are not.

Several universities now run apps designed to help. Students log the moments that confuse them, and the app matches each one to a short explanation written by somebody local. The results so far are modest but encouraging: users report feeling less isolated, although they do not necessarily like the customs any better than before.

The most useful advice comes from people who have moved abroad twice. They say you don't have to understand a rule in order to follow it, and you certainly don't have to agree with it. What you must do is notice it — and the only reliable way to notice an invisible rule is to break it and watch what happens to the room.

Grammar · modals of obligation

PRESENTATION

must / have to — it is necessary: You must show your passport. · I have to work on Saturday.

mustn't — it is forbidden. don't have to — it is not necessary. These are not the same.

should / shouldn't — advice: You should take a small gift.

be supposed to — the rule or expectation, often broken: We're supposed to start at nine.

be allowed to / can — permission: You aren't allowed to take photographs.

Necessary · not necessary

Forbidden · permitted

You have to book a table.

You mustn't take photographs.

You don't have to leave a tip.

You can take photographs.

We must leave before six.

Are we allowed to park here?

You needn't bring anything.

You aren't allowed to smoke inside.

ERROR WARNING

mustn't is not the negative of have to:

You mustn't bring a gift — it's optional. ✗ You don't have to bring a gift. ✓

No to after must: You must to come. ✗ You must come. ✓

must has no past form — use have to: I musted work. ✗ I had to work. ✓

Vocabulary · compound nouns

PRESENTATION

A compound noun is two nouns together. The first one describes the second:

a culture shock · table manners · a dinner party · a dress code

The stress falls on the first word: CULture shock · DINner party · BUSiness card.

They may be one word (homework), two words (culture shock) or hyphenated (son-in-law).
